records.title: 疎行列・非線形方程式系：真の残差を測る
records.section: 疎行列・非線形方程式系：真の残差を測る
records.text: 実装済み：COOからCSRへの組立て、再始動GMRES、BiCGSTAB、Jacobi、ピボット選択なしILU(0)、密行列またはKrylov内部解法を使うArmijo減衰Newton法。内部を確認できる小規模な実数演算の例です。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 疎行列・非線形方程式系：真の残差を測る
records.text:
Saad–Schultz（1986）がGMRES、van der Vorst（1992）がBiCGSTABを導入します。本実装のGMRESはArnoldi再直交化と小さなHessenberg最小二乗問題を使い、指定した内部反復回数で再始動します。BiCGSTABは破綻を明示し、残差は単調に減るとは限りません。
両実装は固定した右前処理を適用します。
A M^{-1} z=b,\qquad x=M^{-1}z,
\qquad \|b-Ax\|_2\leq\max(\mathrm{atol},\mathrm{rtol}\|b\|_2).
停止判定の履歴では真の残差を再計算します。Jacobiは対角スケーリングです。ILU(0)は与えた非ゼロ構造だけを保ち、追加のフィル、ピボット選択、並べ替えを行いません。非常に小さなピボットでは明示的に失敗します。実用的な頑健な疎行列分解を置き換えるものではありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 疎行列・非線形方程式系：真の残差を測る
records.text:
Newton法はJ(x)δ=−F(x)を解き、残差に対するArmijo減少条件を満たすよう後退探索でステップ長を選びます。Newton–Krylovの例はJを組み立ててGMRESを使い、行列不要方式ではありません。Bratu方程式を2つの空間解像度で解析解と比較し、内部求解の失敗も検査します。
残差が小さくても、解誤差が小さいとは限りません。
\frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|}
\leq \kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\hat x\|}{\|b\|}.
条件数、固有値分布、非正規性は異なる性質を表します。条件数が小さいことだけで再始動GMRESの優劣は決められません。CGには引き続き対称正定値演算子と適切な対称正定値前処理が必要で、一般のILU(0)がその条件を満たすとはしていません。
非対称の例は、ゼロDirichlet条件での1次風上移流と中心差分拡散です。1反復あたりの計算量が異なるため、図では実行時間の順位を付けません。データとソースハッシュ、FEMの組立て、陰的ODE段階も参照してください。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.section: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.text: 安定性実験室と実験ガイドで、以下の式をブラウザー内の計算と結び付けて確かめられます。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.section: 空間と時間の離散化を別々に選ぶ#
records.text:
前進差分（forward difference）、後退差分（backward difference）、中心差分（centered difference）は、それぞれ次のように定義します。
D_+u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_j}{h},\qquad
D_-u_j=\frac{u_j-u_{j-1}}h,\qquad
D_0u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_{j-1}}{2h}.
滑らかな関数に対して、前二者は1次、中心差分は2次精度です。numart.advection.finite_differenceで比較できます。線形移流u_t+a u_x=0の風上差分（upwind difference）は情報の伝播方向に従い、a>0では後退差分、a<0では前進差分を使います。したがって、前進差分と風上差分は同じ意味ではありません。
時間方向の前進Euler法はu^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^n、後退Euler法はu^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^{n+1}で、後者では方程式系を解きます。空間に後退差分を使うだけで陰解法になるわけではありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.section: CFL条件と数値的な依存領域#
records.text:
定係数・周期移流を隣接格子点までの陽的差分で解く場合、依存領域の議論から|a|Δt/h ≤ 1が必要です。この定数は差分、Runge–Kutta法、DGの次数、次元によって変わります。陽的拡散にはΔt=O(h²)の制約が現れます。CFL条件は一般に安定性の必要条件であり、十分条件ではありません。Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy（1928）。
時間前進・空間中心差分（FTCS）の移流が反例です。Fourierモードu_j^n=G^n e^{ijθ}を代入すると、
G=1-i C\sin θ,\quad |G|^2=1+C^2\sin^2 θ,
\qquad C=a\Delta t/h.
となり、|C|<1でも増幅するモードがあります。通常のCFL数を固定した格子細分化に対して、この方式は不安定です。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.text:
古典的なLax–Friedrichs法は、
u_j^{n+1}=\tfrac12(u_{j+1}^n+u_{j-1}^n)
-\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n),\qquad
G=\cos θ-iC\sin θ.
です。|G|²=1-(1-C²)sin²θより、この周期線形移流問題では|C|≤1で安定です。古典的LFの数値粘性係数はh/Δtです。Rusanov流束は局所最大波速を使い、本実装のWENOは大域LF流束分割を使います。これらは異なる離散構成です。Lax（1954）。
Lax–Wendroff法は、
u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n-\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n)
+\tfrac{C^2}{2}(u_{j+1}^n-2u_j^n+u_{j-1}^n),
であり、増幅係数は、
G=1-iC\sin θ+C^2(\cos θ-1),\quad
|G|^2=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4(θ/2).
です。この問題での安定条件は同じく|C|≤1です。2次精度であること自体は、不連続近傍の振動を抑える保証にはなりません。Lax–Wendroff（1960）。
テストではamplificationによる解析的な増幅係数と、difference_stepによる実際のモード発展を比較します。図では小さなNyquist摂動を加え、C=0.8とC=1.1を比較しています。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.text:
適切なBanach空間上の適切に設定された線形初期値問題と、整合的な線形差分近似を考えます。固定した有限時間区間で離散発展演算子が一様有界であることを安定性とすると、安定性と収束性は同値です。Lax–Richtmyer（1956）の原論文。
誤差をe^{n+1}=S_h e^n+Δt τ^nと書けば、||S_h^m||≤M_Tから||e^n||≤M_T||e^0||+M_T T max||τ^k||を得ます。整合性により打切り誤差の項がゼロへ向かい、安定性から収束性を導く基本的な議論になります。逆向きには一様有界性の議論が必要です。
この定理から、非線形Euler、WENO、衝撃波、任意の境界処理の正しさを直接保証することはできません。ここでのFourier条件|G|≤1は、周期・定係数のスカラー問題に適用しています。境界、変係数、非正規行列、多段階法には追加の解析が必要です。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 差分、CFL条件、von Neumann解析、Laxの定理
records.section: 初版で用いる時間刻み#
records.text:
Euler系・バロトロピック系：Δt=C h/max(|u|+c)、既定値C=0.3。
DG：Δt=C h/((2p+1)|a|)、既定値C=0.2。
2次元MHD：Δt=C/[max(s_x)/h+max(s_y)/h]、既定値C=0.3。
これらは選定した例で確認した控えめな設定です。すべての初期条件に対する厳密な非線形安定限界ではありません。
A安定性・L安定性とL1／L2／L∞誤差ノルムの定義と比較は、精度と安定性の共通ガイドを参照してください。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 硬い方程式の積分：段階を解き、時間誤差を制御する
records.section: 硬い方程式の積分：段階を解き、時間誤差を制御する
records.text: 実装済み：後退Euler法、その初期化を使う固定刻みBDF2、2段階SDIRK2、1次IMEX Euler、ステップ倍分割による適応SDIRK2。すべての非線形段階に減衰Newton法を使い、失敗を明示します。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 硬い方程式の積分：段階を解き、時間誤差を制御する
records.text:
後退Euler法はy_new−y_old−h f(t_new,y_new)=0を解きます。BDF2は、
\frac{3y_{n+1}-4y_n+y_{n-1}}{2h}=f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1}).
を解きます。ここで使うL安定、2段階、2次精度の単一対角陰的公式の出典はAlexander（1977）です。
\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2,\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&0\\1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},
\quad b=(1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(\gamma,1).
各対角段階は別々の非線形求解です。陰解法では陽解法の安定限界を超える刻みを使える場合がありますが、実用的な刻み幅は精度でも制限されます。収束したNewton残差が測るのは段階方程式であり、時間離散化誤差ではありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 硬い方程式の積分：段階を解き、時間誤差を制御する
records.text:
適応実装はSDIRK2の1全ステップと2半ステップを比べます。局所誤差推定は(y_half−y_full)/3で、atol+rtol max(|y_old|,|y_half|)で尺度化します。Richardson外挿はせず、2半ステップの値を採用し、指数−1/3でhを調整します。棄却試行と受理ステップを数え、試行上限に達するとエラーにします。
IMEX Eulerは一方を陽的、他方を陰的に評価します。この最小の1次分割は、Ascher–Ruuth–Spiteri（1997）の高次IMEX RK構成ではありません。陽的部分には独自の安定制約が残ります。可変刻みBDF、埋込みDIRK対、演算子分割は今後の拡張です。
硬いテストy′=−1000(y−cos t)−sin tは、y(0)=1のとき厳密解cos tを持ちます。計算記録は、実際の積分節点での最大誤差と適応ステップ数を残します。別のテストで、非線形・非自律ODEの次数と、硬い減衰モードの強い減衰を確認します。
外力付きの硬い問題の粗い刻み列は、一様な2次収束の範囲にはありません。BDF2の開始処理と硬い系の次数低下が、節点全体の最大誤差へ影響します。形式的な時間次数は、非線形・非硬性の次数テストで別に確認します。
A安定性・L安定性とL1／L2／L∞誤差ノルムは、精度と安定性の共通ガイドを参照してください。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.section: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.text: シンプレクティック積分器は正準2形式を保ちながらHamilton系を進めます。多くの軌道・粒子積分の良い長時間挙動を支える写像の性質ですが、元のHamiltonianを一般に厳密保存するわけではありません。Hamilton写像ノートは2つの問いを計算例で分けます。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.text:
状態z=(q,p)に対し、Hamilton方程式とシンプレクティック条件は、
\dot z=J\nabla H(z),\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad D\Phi_h(z)^T J D\Phi_h(z)=J.
です。最後の恒等式は各数値ステップが正準変換であることを示します。1自由度ではdet(D Phi)=1と同値で、向き付き位相面積を保ちます。高次元で総体積だけを保つ条件は、それより弱いものです。
2形式の保存、Hの保存、時間対称性Phi_(−h)=Phi_h^(−1)を別々に検査します。シンプレクティックEulerはその違いの例で、一般に厳密エネルギー保存でも時間対称でもありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.section: Hamiltonianを分けて厳密な部分流を合成する#
records.text:
単位質量の可分系H(q,p)=p²/2+V(q)では、2つの部分流はドリフトとキックです。
D_h(q,p)=(q+hp,p),\qquad K_h(q,p)=(q,p-h\nabla V(q)).
それぞれがシンプレクティックで、合成もそうなります。ノートにはkick–driftのシンプレクティックEulerと、対称2次のStörmer–Verlet、
p_{n+1/2}=p_n-\frac h2\nabla V(q_n),\quad
q_{n+1}=q_n+h p_{n+1/2},\quad
p_{n+1}=p_{n+1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1}).
があります。これは力学のleapfrog／速度Verletで、時間積分ノートの2ステップスカラー漸化式とは異なります。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.text:
VerletステップをS2(h)とすると、4次合成の一例は、
S_4(h)=S_2(a h)\,S_2(b h)\,S_2(a h),\qquad
a=\frac1{2-2^{1/3}},\quad b=-\frac{2^{1/3}}{2-2^{1/3}}.
です。Yoshida（1990）は高次シンプレクティック合成を発展させます。bが負なので内部部分ステップは時間を逆行します。ここでの滑らかな保存系には適しますが、不可逆な拡散、衝撃波、衝突処理へ単に適用することは正当化されません。高次でも無条件安定や同一コストの優位性は示せません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.text:
後退誤差解析は近傍の、一般には形式的な修正Hamiltonianを記述します。滑らかさ、有界軌道、小刻みなどの仮定で、小さな長時間エネルギー誤差を説明できます。すべての軌道・刻みで元のHが厳密不変とはしません。Hairer・Lubich・Wanner（2003）が幾何学的な視点と仮定を論じます。
特別な振動子H=(p²+q²)/2では、kick–drift–kick Verletは、
I_h=\frac12p^2+\frac12\left(1-\frac{h^2}{4}\right)q^2
を丸め誤差まで保存し、H自体は振動します。この不変量から、係数を変えていないHamiltonian流が厳密に数値の時間h写像だとは言えません。|h|<2では有界ですが、それを超えるとシンプレクティックなまま不安定になり得ます。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.text:
陰的中点則は端点方程式を正確に解くとシンプレクティックかつ時間対称です。この2次振動子ではHを丸め誤差まで保存しますが、非2次Hを厳密保存するとは限りません。古典的RK4は4次ですが、一般にはシンプレクティックでも時間対称でもありません。短時間精度の良さだけでは写像の幾何は保証されません。
第2問題はH=p²/2+q²/2+q⁴/4という滑らかな非線形振動子です。中点則の特別な2次エネルギー保存と一般的主張の違いが見えるようになります。

records.title: シンプレクティック積分：正準写像とエネルギーを分ける
records.section: 再現可能なノートと検査#
records.text:
from numart.hamiltonian import trajectory, energy, canonical_step, J
t, z = trajectory(h=0.2, steps=1000, method='yoshida4', system='quartic')
print(max(abs((energy(z, 'quartic')-energy(z[0], 'quartic'))/energy(z[0], 'quartic'))))
_, M = canonical_step([0.7, 0.4], 0.2, 'yoshida4', 'quartic', True)
print(M.T @ J @ M - J)
計算データとソース記録は、5手法、2つのHamiltonian、h=0.1、0.2、0.4の30軌道を、(q,p)=(1,0.2)からT=200まで供給します。描画軌道は最大1001標本ですが、最大エネルギー誤差は全積分ステップを使います。位相パッチは(0.7,0.4)中心の正方形へ1ステップ作用させます。標本多角形は図示で、局所欠損は中心の解析的な写像Jacobianを使います。
テストは厳密振動子に対する収束、解析Jacobianと独立差分、両ポテンシャルの正準恒等式、対称法の時間反転、Verletの2次不変量、中点則の2次・非2次エネルギーの違いを確認します。教育用固定刻み例であり、軌道精度や時間コストの順位ではありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.text: 空間再構成と時間積分は独立した選択です。空間離散化後、PDEはODE系dU/dt = L(U)になります。精度、安定性、単調性、散逸、計算量は両者に依存します。時間積分ノートではy′=i y、y(0)=1を使い、時間積分の選択を切り分けます。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.section: ひとつの振動子と12手法#
records.text:
厳密解exp(i t)は単位円をたどります。前進Eulerと後退Eulerは1次精度で、この無減衰振動子に対して前者は増幅、後者は減衰します。陽的RK2にはHeun／SSPRK(2,2)、陽的中点、Ralstonがあります。Kutta RK3、SSPRK(3,3)、SSPRK(4,3)は3次、古典的RK4とSSPRK(5,4)は4次です。陰的中点則は2次で、この線形振動子の振幅を保存しますが、位相には誤差があります。RK系譜の章と系譜ノートで段数・次数・SSP、非線形テストを比較できます。
y′=lambda yに対してz=lambda delta tと置くと、1ステップ増幅係数の例は、
R_{\rm FE}=1+z,\quad R_{\rm BE}=\frac1{1-z},\quad
R_{\rm midpoint}=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2}.
です。このスカラー線形方程式では、3種のRK2、Kutta RK3／SSPRK(3,3)、古典的RK4のRK係数は、それぞれ2次、3次、4次までの指数関数のTaylor多項式になります。SSPRK(4,3)には4次項z⁴/48、SSPRK(5,4)には5次項もあります。同じスカラー増幅係数でも、非線形RK段階が同じとは限りません。SSP性は空間演算子の前進Euler限界に依存し、無条件安定ではありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.text:
1階の方程式系を中心差分で進める2ステップ漸化式は、
y^{n+1}=y^{n-1}+2z y^n,\qquad
\xi_\pm=z\pm\sqrt{1+z^2}.
です。zがゼロへ向かうと+1へ近づく根が物理モード、−1へ近づく根がステップごとに交互に変わる計算モードを担います。両方の根と重複度が重要です。z=i sigmaでは、|sigma|<1なら異なる2根の絶対値は1です。|sigma|=1では重根によって線形増大する解があり得るため、一般的な有界性の主張に端点を含めてはいけません。その上では一方の根が等比的に増幅します。
y(0)に加えて開始値が必要です。本実装ではRK4で1ステップ進め、必要に応じてy(1)へ実摂動epsilonを加えます。lambda=0なら、偶数番目の標本は1、奇数番目は1+epsilonとなり、計算モードを直接示せます。ノートの振動子では物理モードも同時に変化します。
Robert–Asselin系などの時間フィルターは、減衰と精度のトレードオフを伴って挙動を変えます。Williams（2009）を参照してください。初版にはフィルターを適用していません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.text: 位置と速度をずらして更新するkick–drift法や、2階の力学系に対する速度Verletも、leapfrogと呼ばれることがあります。変数が異なる時刻位置にあり、シンプレクティックな解釈にはその構造を使います。上のスカラー漸化式は、完全なSPH粒子積分器の実演でも、一般の力学系の長時間エネルギー保存の証明でもありません。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.section: ノートを再現して読む#
records.text:
from numart.time_integration import linear_trajectory, leapfrog_roots
t, y = linear_trajectory(rate=1j, dt=0.1, steps=200, method='leapfrog')
print(leapfrog_roots(0.1j))
ブラウザーでは、終了時刻20でPython計算した軌道から、12手法、7刻み幅、leapfrog開始摂動3種を選べます。不安定な標本では軸範囲が広がります。陰的求解とRK段数が異なるため、同じ時間区間でも同じ計算量とは限りません。テストでは時間収束次数、leapfrogの根、交互モード、中点則の振幅を確認します。
これらの振動子軌道はスカラー安定性係数を評価し、この線形テスト方程式ではRK段階と代数的に等価です。別の系譜ノートでは完全な非線形段階を評価します。空間安定性実験室、SPH、ALEへ進んでください。
records.notice: 日本語訳はドラフトです。数式・計算・参照資料は英語原文と照合できます。

records.title: 時間積分とleapfrog法
records.text: シンプレクティック積分の章では、調和・4次Hamilton系に対して、力学的なkick–drift–kick Verlet、吉田の4次合成、シンプレクティックEuler、陰的中点則を実装します。写像ノートではRK4と比較し、正準構造と厳密なエネルギー保存を分けます。

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.text: Companion reading / Interfaces across disciplines

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.section:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.text:
Bistability, diffusion and an integral selection condition also organize biological patterns. These primary-source comparisons distinguish shared mathematics from different physical mechanisms.
These are companion references, separate from the thermal-instability paper atlas. No biological simulation or quantitative cross-model reproduction is claimed. Our mathematical comparison uses the KI/ZP saturation benchmark and Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992).

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.section: Closest match: wave-pinning in cell polarity.
records.text:
Mori, Jilkine & Edelstein-Keshet (2008), Wave-Pinning and Cell Polarity from a Bistable Reaction-Diffusion System, Biophysical Journal 94, 3684–3697, models slowly diffusing active membrane protein exchanging with a rapidly diffusing inactive pool. Total protein is conserved. An activation front consumes the pool and stops as that pool reaches a critical value.
Equations (10)–(11) and Figure 3 explicitly give a zero-reaction-integral condition, called a Maxwell condition. The near-uniform inactive concentration plays the role of a front-selection parameter; total mass also fixes the eventual front position. In ZP saturation, the selector is pressure and the integral carries the conductivity weight. This is a comparison of selection conditions, not an identification of protein diffusion with thermal conduction.
Biological front: I(b*) = ∫[a− → a+] f(a,b*) da = 0
Planar ZP front: ∫[Tc → Tw] κ(T) Q(T,P_sat) dT = 0
Mori, Jilkine & Edelstein-Keshet (2011), Asymptotic and Bifurcation Analysis of Wave-Pinning in a Reaction-Diffusion Model for Cell Polarization, SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 71, 1401–1427, analyzes the stationary front, its asymptotic regime and loss through bifurcations. It is the follow-up for evaluating diffusion ratios, total mass and persistence. Author-hosted published paper.

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.section: Closest match: wave-pinning in cell polarity.
records.text: Possible small benchmark: compute the reaction integral and stationary front first, then let the conserved pool evolve. This would separate a static selector from the mechanism that drives the system toward it. No benchmark has yet been implemented.

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.text:
Brauns, Halatek & Frey (2020), Phase-Space Geometry of Mass-Conserving Reaction-Diffusion Dynamics, Physical Review X 10, 041036, develops local reactive equilibria, diffusion-driven mass redistribution and stationary flux balance for two-component protein-pattern models.
Section III E, equations (16)–(20), selects stationary profiles by zero total reactive turnover. Equation (17) is a reaction-integral balance. Its interpretation as equal geometric areas between a nullcline and a flux-balance line requires additional approximations, stated before equation (19). This is especially relevant to comparing saturation conditions: identify the variable, weight and conserved quantity before drawing equal areas.
The correspondence with thermal fronts is our comparison. These multicomponent dynamics should not automatically be assigned a scalar Ginzburg–Landau free energy. Open-access original paper.

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.section: A related, distinct branch: neural excitability.
records.text:
FitzHugh (1961), Impulses and Physiological States in Theoretical Models of Nerve Membrane, Biophysical Journal 1, 445–466, introduces a two-variable model of excitation and refractoriness, a foundation of the FitzHugh–Nagumo family. Its nullcline geometry and threshold dynamics provide a connection to reduced nonlinear models.
Excitable pulses involve activation followed by recovery. A cubic fast subsystem can resemble a bistable front problem when the slow variable is frozen; a full pulse is not simply a static wall between two thermally stable phases. This is a weaker analogy than wave-pinning for the present saturation-pressure question. The reference was checked at the bibliography and abstract level; its detailed equations and travelling-wave reductions have not been audited here.

records.title:
When a moving
biological front stops.
records.text:
Retain the number of fields, the conserved quantity, the transport law, the control parameter and the reason a front stops. Protein total-mass conservation and gas mass conservation do not make temperature a conserved order parameter. A geometric resemblance between curves alone does not establish the same instability or the same stationary-front criterion.
The Elphick/Ginzburg–Landau connection supplies the reduced thermal-front functional; Maxwell’s historical construction supplies the thermodynamic comparison. These companion references extend the discussion without treating biological pattern formation as a reproduction of an interstellar calculation.
Sources checked 3 November 2026. Bibliography, reviewed sections and limits / JSON. The four companion papers are linked here; only the explicitly requested Elphick paper has been added to the main thermal-instability catalog.

records.section: Maxwell’s rule on a van der Waals isotherm.
records.text:
For molar volume v, the van der Waals equation is p(T,v) = RT/(v − b) − a/v². The attraction term and excluded volume can give a loop below the critical temperature. At a fixed temperature, Maxwell’s construction selects the liquid–vapour coexistence pressure by balancing signed areas on the pressure–volume diagram:
p(T, v_liquid) = p(T, v_vapour) = p_coexist
∫[v_liquid → v_vapour] [p(T,v) − p_coexist] dv = 0
In modern thermodynamic terms, the two phases share temperature, pressure and chemical potential. The horizontal segment represents changing phase fractions. The mechanically unstable portion of the homogeneous loop is bypassed. Equal areas are coordinate dependent: replacing volume by density requires the inverse-square Jacobian; equal-looking areas on a pressure–density plot do not give the same rule.
Maxwell’s 1875 paper explicitly describes a horizontal line cutting equal areas from an isothermal curve, using a reversible-cycle work argument. The transcription of the original Chemical Society paper preserves that argument. The construction is properly called Maxwell’s equal-area rule, applied here to a van der Waals equation of state.

records.section: ZP saturation balances a different integral.
records.text:
The cold and warm interstellar phases have different temperatures and are maintained by external heating and radiative cooling. With net volumetric cooling Q = n²Λ − nΓ, a static planar conductive front satisfies:
F = κ(T) dT/dx
F dF/dT = κ(T) Q(T,P)
F(T_cold) = F(T_warm) = 0
∫[T_cold → T_warm] κ(T) Q(T,P_sat) dT = 0
This derivation assumes a static planar front with no mass flux and the specified local cooling law and conductivity. It is an energy-transport selection condition. Thermodynamic liquid–vapour coexistence does not directly supply this pressure. The analogy is cancellation of signed integrals; the ZP condition includes a conductivity weight and integrates over temperature. A Maxwell construction on the interstellar pressure–density equilibrium curve would generally select a different value.
For the corrected KI2002 fit with κ = 2500√T, our computed benchmark gives Psat/kB = 2822.884297 K cm⁻³, with cold and warm endpoints at 54.980188 K and 6417.132178 K. No molecular van der Waals force is added to that gas model.

records.title:
Two phases.
Which area must balance?
records.text:
A bistable reaction–diffusion equation can have the structure of real, overdamped time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau relaxation. Two stable thermal phases correspond to two potential minima; the unstable equilibrium lies between them. An interface is a domain wall. Equal well depths permit a static planar wall; unequal depths drive its motion.
Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992), Dynamics of Fronts in Thermally Bistable Fluids, ApJ 392, 106–117, provide a direct precedent. Their isobaric one-dimensional reduction uses a Lagrangian mass coordinate m. Equations (2.14) and (3.2)–(3.3) have the following dimensionless gradient-flow form:
Z_t = F(Z) + Z^β Z_mm = −Z^β δE/δZ
G(Z,p) = Z^(−β) F(Z,p) = −∂U/∂Z
E[Z] = ∫ [½ (∂Z/∂m)² + U(Z,p)] dm
Z = T^α, β = (α − 1)/α, κ ∝ T^α
For positive temperature the mobility Z^β is positive. With vanishing boundary terms, dE/dt = −∫ Z^(−β) (Z_t)² dm ≤ 0. Their Figure 1 and page 109 explicitly connect equal potential minima with a stationary ZP kink. This source includes fluid motion within the isobaric reduction; it does not reduce the entire compressible problem to an arbitrary scalar equation.
A qualitative illustration from phase.avi. Surrounding axes are cropped; the recording has not been matched to the reduced equation discussed here.

records.section: Recover the ZP condition directly from the static equation.
records.text:
The following change of variable is our derivation from the static front equation, rather than a claim that the paper uses the same variable or potential normalization:
θ(T) = ∫ κ(T) dT
θ_xx = Q(T(θ), P)
V(θ;P) = ∫ Q(T(θ), P) dθ
V(θ_warm;P) − V(θ_cold;P)
 = ∫[T_cold → T_warm] κ(T) Q(T,P) dT
At Psat the last integral vanishes: the two minima have equal depths. At a uniform equilibrium, V″ = (∂Q/∂T)P / κ, so the isobarically stable branches are potential minima. For a formal scalar relaxation θ_t = M(θ)[θ_xx − ∂V/∂θ] with M > 0, the same static equation is stationary. This construction establishes the static mathematical correspondence; it does not derive the full time-dependent gas dynamics.
A symmetric quartic double well is a useful cubic-reaction illustration. The KI cooling law is not exactly cubic, and its equal-depth wells need not be mirror symmetric. The functional above is an effective Lyapunov functional of a reduced, externally heated and radiatively cooled system; it is not identified with the equilibrium thermodynamic free energy of the gas. The analogy concerns a real scalar relaxation model, not the full complex order parameter and electromagnetic structure of superconducting Ginzburg–Landau theory. Temperature is not a conserved order parameter, while the underlying gas still conserves mass.

Source review, 3 November 2026: publisher metadata for both Nature installments and the 1874 review were checked; the equal-area passage was read in the transcription of Maxwell’s original paper. This aside makes no claim to reconstruct the original diagrams or establish publication priority among all earlier works.

records.section: How much ionization energy becomes heat?
records.text:
Derived diagnostics from GHF (1969), equations (25)–(26), printed p. 181. Both curves depend on x = ne/n(H I). Their denominators differ: energy per primary liberated electron is not the same quantity as the fraction of total ionization-plus-excitation losses.SVGPNGHeating data / CSVQ(x) = (1 + 130x)/(1 + 57x)
eh = 9Q eV   ·   f = 0.13Q
The electron fraction changes how energetic electrons share their energy with the gas. Equation (26) gives approximately 9, 13, and 20 eV at x = 10⁻⁴, 10⁻², and 1. The printed fit slightly exceeds 20 eV near x = 1; the code preserves the historical rounded expression.
Equation (23) separately gives Γion/(ζntarget) = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹Q erg. Here ntarget = n(H I) + n(He I) + n(He II) is the density of primary-ionization targets in equation (20), distinct from the H+He nuclei density n0, and ζ is the cosmic-ray ionization rate. Direct electron heating is another term, Γel = 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁰neζ erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹. It is not added to the plotted energy without specifying the particle populations.
Rounded coefficients in the paper are retained independently: the 0.13 in equation (25) is not forced to equal 1.4/11 from the prefactors of equations (23)–(24).

records.section: Six model choices, one explicit temperature window.
records.text:
Solutions for n₀ = 1–1,000 cm⁻³, searched within T = 10–2,000 K. Colors identify the normal abundance and FGH Letter depletion cases. Solid curves include electrons from singly ionized C, Si, and Fe; dashed curves use H/He charge only. Missing segments have no sign-changing root in the chosen window. No thermal-stability classification is assigned.SVGPNGSolutions & energy budgets / CSVModel choices / JSON
At n₀ = 100 cm⁻³, the version with C+Si+Fe electrons gives approximately 19.22 K for normal abundances, 38.07 K for case a, and 63.34 K for case b. These are results of this reduced model. The calculation has not been tuned to match an original curve.
Depletion reduces the available metal cooling. At the same density the gas must reach a higher temperature before cooling balances heating. The electron-donor comparison isolates a second input choice while leaving the other assumptions fixed.

records.title:
Find a cold branch.
Keep the assumptions visible.
records.text:
At each trial density and temperature, a monotone bisection solves charge neutrality and the primary ionization/recombination equilibria of H and He. A logarithmic temperature scan identifies sign changes in the net energy loss; bisection then refines each bracket. All sign-changing roots found are retained in the CSV.
ζn(H I) = αB(T)nen(H II)
ne = n(H II) + n(He II) + 2n(He III) + nmetal,e
Γ = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹Q(x)ζntarget + 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁰neζ
Λmetals + Λrecombination + Λfree-free = Γ
Here ζ = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ s⁻¹, x = ne/n(H I), Q = (1+130x)/(1+57x), and ntarget = n(H I)+n(He I)+n(He II). This target sum differs from n₀, which counts all H+He nuclei. Heating and cooling are volumetric rates in erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹. The pressure proxy (n₀+ne)T omits trace-element nuclei.
H/He recombination uses the excited-state fits obtained by subtracting Hjellming’s ground-state coefficients from his total coefficients. Recombination kinetic-energy loss follows his energy-weighted definition. The hydrogenic He approximation is a historical approximation whose accuracy at cold-gas temperatures remains to be assessed.

records.section: Read the model before interpreting the curves.
records.text:
Ionization: equal primary rates for H I, He I, and He II; no secondary-electron ionization or thermal collisional ionization.
Cooling: tabulated metal channels, recombination, and free-free emission. Thermal H/He excitation, molecules, grains, and stellar heating are absent. Blank Table 1 channels are omitted inputs, not measured zeros.
Populations: low-density excitation with all C, Si, and Fe singly ionized and O neutral. Each listed transition uses the whole elemental population; no level statistical-equilibrium calculation is included.
Composition: He is 10% of H+He nuclei. Per million H nuclei, C=300, O=670, Si=30, Fe=8, transcribed from Field et al. (1968), Table 1, which cites Allen (1963). We have not directly checked Allen’s book.
Depletion: the FGH Letter divisors are selected explicitly. The different values in the companion GHF paper remain recorded in the source audit.
Search: roots outside 10–2,000 K are outside this calculation. Tangential roots can evade a sign-change scan. Scan refinement checks the reported numerical roots, without proving global completeness.
Curves under these assumptions do not establish the original two-phase pressure interval or a warm branch. Later microphysics will be tracked through Wolfire and GOW references.

GHF Table 1, the equation (13) heating coefficients, and the Field et al. (1968) abundance baseline were visually rechecked. No transcription error was found in these inputs. The earlier Fe cascade discussion also cautions against adding extra lower-level population factors to coefficients that describe total excitation losses.
At the text’s n = 0.21 cm⁻³, T = 7,800 K point, the implemented cooling is 1.171 times the heating. Si II supplies about 31.4% of model cooling and the O I 22,500-K term about 18.0%. The downloadable report separates every heating and cooling contribution.
One-term sensitivity probes do not identify a correction: halving or doubling thermal Lyman-alpha cooling shifts the warm pressure maximum by only about +1.6% or −1.9%; applying the printed GHF 2/3 recombination-energy factor shifts it by less than 1%. These are diagnostics, not recovered cross sections, uncertainty bounds, or alternative fits to the original curve.

records.section: What changed from the reduced cold branch?
records.text:
The solver now includes cosmic-ray production and removal of 20-eV superthermal electrons, secondary hydrogen ionization, thermal hydrogen excitation and ionization, and direct electron heating. These interact with H/He recombination, charge neutrality, historical metal cooling, and free-free emission.
ζ[n(H I) + n(He I) + n(He II)]
= nfast[n(H I)(q′ion + q′ex) + neq′ee]
Γindirect = nfast[3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ n(H I) + 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁷ ne]
These follow GHF equations (13) and (20). Heating is evaluated directly from the superthermal population, with ζ = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ s⁻¹. The closure uses the printed H/He charge balance, without added metal-donor electrons. The earlier primary-only cold-branch calculation remains available to inspect that approximation separately.

records.title:

records.text:
GHF p. 178 prints the hydrogen ionization triangle: threshold 13.6 eV, peak cross section 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ cm² at 50 eV, and zero at 300 eV. Its Maxwellian average is integrated analytically and checked against independent numerical quadrature.
The same page does not print the complete Lyman-alpha fit, referring instead to Fite, Stebbings & Brackmann (1959) and Goldsmith’s Berkeley thesis (1969). We infer the excitation cross section at 20 eV from rounded equations (12)–(13), after subtracting the explicit ionization contribution. A linear rise from the 10.2-eV threshold is an assumption; it has not been validated against those data.
Two alternative tails beyond 20 eV change the calculated density at fixed temperature by at most about 0.13% over the sampled roots. That small sensitivity does not validate the assumed threshold slope or its normalization. The separate recombination-energy convention test changes density by at most about 0.65%.
Thermal He excitation and ionization are omitted. He I recombination uses the hydrogen approximation; metal cooling uses a low-density sum without level statistical equilibrium. The full list is in the configuration and limitations. The figure uses historical inputs with these declared approximations; it does not substitute a modern KI or Wolfire cooling fit.

sets a small-scale limit.
records.text: For this choice of α, the gas is stable to an isochoric perturbation but unstable to isobaric condensation. At small wavenumber, the finite sound speed limits the growth; the normalized rate tends to zero linearly with wavenumber.

records.title:

records.text: From the paper to the calculation

records.title:
How thermal conduction
sets a small-scale limit.
records.text:
Field writes perturbations as exp(nt + i k·r): positive real n means growth. Using equations (27) and (38), define q = k/kρ, x = n/(kρc), α = kT/kρ, and β = kρ/kK. Here c is the adiabatic sound speed and the three characteristic wavenumbers are defined by equation (16).
x³ + (α + βq²)x² + q²x + q²(α − 1 + βq²)/γ = 0
Equation (39), regrouped as a cubic in x. The heat-loss function is energy losses minus gains per unit mass per unit time. β = 0 is the zero-conductivity limit. These normalizations assume kρ > 0, as in Figure 2.
For these parameters the polynomial is strictly increasing for nonnegative x. Within the unstable band it has exactly one positive root, which the code finds by bisection. At q = 0 it uses the limiting value x = 0.
For β > 0, the neutral cutoff is qc = √[(1 − α)/β]: approximately 7.0711, 2.2361, and 0.7071 for β = 0.01, 0.1, and 1. The first lies just beyond the plotted range, as in the original figure. Stable-domain growth values are left blank in the CSV.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.text: Field (1965), Figure 1, printed p. 536; γ = 5/3. Color indicates the number of roots with positive real part, counted with multiplicity. Hatching means three real distinct roots. Neutral lines are treated separately. The circular annotation guide in the original is omitted because it is not a stability boundary.SVG figurePNG figureDomain grid / CSVConductive paths / CSVValidation / JSON

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.section: Conduction is already on the horizontal axis.
records.text:
Equation (17) defines y = n/(kc), σρ = kρ/k, and σT′ = kT/k + k/kK. The horizontal coordinate includes the positive thermal-conduction contribution. Both coordinates and y are dimensionless; c is the adiabatic sound speed.
y³ + σT′y² + y + (σT′ − σρ)/γ = 0
Equation (18). This normalization uses kc; Figures 2 and 3 instead use kρc.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.text: The solid line σρ = σT′ has a zero root and is the isobaric neutral line. The dashed line σρ = −(γ − 1)σT′ has purely imaginary roots and is the isentropic neutral line.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.text: The discriminant boundary changes the character of the roots. Inside the hatching, all three roots are real and distinct. Outside, there is one real root and a complex conjugate pair. The hatching is not an additional instability threshold.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.text:
A growing root means Re(y) > 0. A complex conjugate pair with positive real part counts as two growing roots. Away from neutral lines, the count is:
N = 1[σρ > σT′]
+ 2[σρ < −(γ − 1)σT′]
Here 1[condition] is 1 when the condition is true, otherwise 0. On neutral lines the CSV leaves N blank, so zero-real-part roots are not classified by an off-boundary rule.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.text:
Write t = σT′ and r = σρ. Field’s equation (19) defines:
D = [(t − r)/γ − t/3 + 2t³/27]²/4
+ [1 − t²/3]³/27
For this definition, D < 0 gives three real roots, while D > 0 gives a complex pair. The conventional cubic discriminant is −108D, with the opposite sign. Equation (20) supplies the thorn boundaries; their tips are triple roots at t = ±√3, r = (1 − γ/9)t.

records.title: A map of growing modes.
records.section: Follow a path into Figures 2 and 3.
records.text:
With q = k/kρ > 0, equation (28) gives r = 1/q and t = α/q + βq = αr + β/r. The green paths use α = 1/2, as in Figure 2; the brown paths use α = −2, as in Figure 3. Each family has β = 0.01, 0.1, 1, with dotted zero-conduction reference rays.
Increasing wavenumber moves toward smaller positive r. Conduction shifts the path to the right, where it can cross the neutral lines. The growth-rate normalization converts as x = qy. The validation checks this mapping using all three roots along each conducting path.
A path can cross the wave neutral line while condensation is still unstable. The map counts all growing roots; the wave cutoff in Figure 3 concerns only the acoustic pair.

records.title: When sound waves grow.
records.text: Write x = ξ + iη, with time normalized by kρc. The real part ξ sets the exponential growth or decay of the disturbance. Positive ξ is an oscillatory instability, also called overstability.

records.title: When sound waves grow.
records.text: The two conjugate roots have opposite frequencies and equal growth rates. The code keeps the positive-frequency member, η > 0. The figure plots ξ; the CSV retains both ξ and η.

records.title: When sound waves grow.
records.text: At long wavelengths, Re(x) tends to zero quadratically with q = k/kρ. Without conduction it approaches 0.1 at short wavelengths. Increasing conduction reduces growth and introduces a finite wave cutoff.

records.title: When sound waves grow.
records.section: The growing wave is not the fastest root.
records.text:
As in Figure 2, define x = n/(kρc), q = k/kρ, α = kT/kρ, β = kρ/kK, and s = α + βq². The same dispersion relation applies:
x³ + sx² + q²x + q²(s − 1)/γ = 0
At q = 0, the wave pair tends to x = 0, whereas the condensation root tends to −α = 2. Selecting the root with the largest real part would draw the condensation mode instead of Figure 3. The script identifies the unique root with positive imaginary part and fails if no unique wave pair exists.
Equation (40) provides a separate check on ξ = Re(x):
ξ³ + sξ² + (s² + q²)ξ/4
+ q²[(1 − 1/γ)s + 1/γ]/8 = 0

records.title: When sound waves grow.
records.section: A damped wave can coexist with condensation.
records.text:
The wave cutoff follows equation (26): qc = √[(−α − 1/(γ − 1))/β] = √(0.5/β). For β = 0.01, 0.1, and 1 this is approximately 7.0711, 2.2361, and 0.7071. The first is just outside the plotted interval.
At the cutoff, s = −1.5 and the cubic factors as (x + s)(x² + q²). The wave roots are purely imaginary, x = ±iq, but the condensation root remains x = 1.5.
The wave mode is damped above its cutoff. This does not imply stability of the whole gas: for these parameters the condensation mode remains unstable until a higher wavenumber.

They are effective visual demonstrations at compact gallery sizes. Their native resolutions are 500–800 pixels wide and their cadences are 3–10 fps. This identifies the caption on the recording; it does not establish a match to a specific paper figure, simulation dimensionality in that paper, or verified numerical parameters. The 2D titles here describe the visible panels and evolution. A number in a filename is not treated as a confirmed computational mesh size.
The gallery was curated from 87 video files, representing 55 byte-distinct recordings after SHA-256 deduplication. Astronomy candidates were visually inspected at several times. The eight selected originals and their MP4 derivatives were decoded completely; dimensions and frame counts were checked. These are technical media checks, not numerical or physical validation of the simulations.

records.section:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.text:
A pressure and a mass flux can select very different connections between cold and warm gas. We solve the steady front equations behind the paper’s classification diagrams, starting from the cold neutral medium.
This is a computed subset prepared for technical review, not a completed reproduction of every published region or auxiliary curve. Nine published example classifications agree. The map marks unavailable CNM branches and unresolved or temperature-limited cases instead of filling them from the source figure.

records.title:

records.section:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.text: The KI2002 equilibrium benchmark documents the corrected coefficients used here, stable and unstable branches, and all three equilibrium intersections at the ZP saturation pressure.

records.title:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.section: Toward Figure 5: pressure and condensation flux.
records.text:
29 pressure samples × 45 flux samples. Each cell is computed from the printed model. The white dashed curve is the condensation ZP separatrix, found by matching phase integrations from the cold and warm equilibria. Gray inputs lack the outgoing CNM saddle on the implemented density branch. White is unresolved. The source jcrit overlay remains to be audited.PNGSVGAll decisions / CSVComputed boundaries / CSV
C–U–o approaches unstable gas with a temperature overshoot; C–U approaches it monotonically. C–c reaches the critical point, while C–C connects cold equilibria. A local node at the unstable equilibrium is insufficient to establish C–U: the paper explicitly notes that the global trajectory can still overshoot.
The condensation flux is plotted as −j divided by mH × (1 cm⁻³) × (1 km s⁻¹). Positive plotted values therefore mean negative physical j. The physical mass flux has units g cm⁻² s⁻¹; the density unit implicit in the source’s compact axis label is explicit here.

records.title:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.section: Toward Figure 7: extend the pressure range.
records.text:
33 × 49 samples. The dark dashed curve marks Tcrit = 10,000 K. Here the white region consists of 669 samples with no terminal point inside the declared 20,000 K search window; it is not assigned a physical class by extrapolating the rate fit. It must not be read as an absence of steady solutions in the paper.PNGSVGAll decisions / CSVComputed boundaries / CSV
The published Figure 7 extends beyond the bistable-pressure interval. This prototype keeps a temperature window and an explicit CNM boundary branch; those restrictions explain much of the difference in displayed coverage. The exported decisions distinguish restricted coverage from the paper’s classifications.

records.title:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.text:
Equations (5)–(7) set the thermal equilibrium curve. Equation (16), the conductivity-weighted net-loss integral, selects the saturation pressure.Equilibrium data / CSVSVG
The printed cooling fit gives Pmin/kB = 1,597.45, Pmax/kB = 5,007.00, and Psat/kB = 2,822.88 K cm⁻³. The source quotes 1596 in the text / 1598 in Figure 1, 5012, and 2823. These small differences are retained.
At Pc/kB = 3,000 K cm⁻³, the matched condensation ZP flux is −j = 0.00315993 in the plotted normalization, close to the quoted 0.0032. The calculation preserves constant mass and momentum flux and uses the full plus-density branch of equation (11), rather than imposing constant pressure throughout the front.

records.title:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.text:
ρv = j   ·   ρv² + P = M
ρ(T) = [M + √(M²−4ℛj²T)]/(2ℛT)
d(F²)/dT = ℛj[(γ+1)/(γ−1)+M/√(M²−4ℛj²T)]F + 2κρℒ
Here dθ = κdT and F = dθ/dx = κdT/dx. The physical conductive heat flux is −F. The CNM boundary is a thermal equilibrium with F = 0, approached along its outgoing saddle eigenvector. The source heating/cooling fit, pure atomic hydrogen, γ = 5/3, and κ = 2500√T are used.
For node-like targets, the solver follows log(F) and refines the remaining temperature distance. A captured trajectory has F proportional to that distance; a crossing retains finite F. Two consecutive refinements must agree. Ambiguous cases remain white. Grid boundaries have not been digitized against the published figure.

records.title:
Classify the interface
by following its trajectory.
records.section: Two implementation questions to discuss with the authors.
records.text:
Continuation of the CNM boundary: at large imposed flux, the implemented plus-density branch can lose its outgoing CNM saddle. How should the boundary or branch be continued to recover the rest of the published C–C coverage?
The reference state for jcrit: what temperature interval and loss normalization were used to choose Tm in section 4.1.2? The prototype does not infer an unprinted selection, so it omits that overlay.
These are questions about the present implementation and interpretation. They are not assertions of errors in the paper. A useful first review package is this page, the nine example checks, the source audit, and the two grid CSVs.
The first technical milestone is agreement on these model choices. Quantitative boundary comparisons, finer sampling, and broader continuation can then follow. The front lineage provides the context connecting Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner, Penston–Brown, Nagashima, and later front studies.

records.text:
Balance heating and cooling, follow the stable and unstable branches, and locate the pressure that supports a static planar conductive front.
A new diagnostic of the corrected model, with numerical validation. This does not reproduce the original two-dimensional simulation or claim to digitize an equilibrium figure from the 2002 paper. The same cooling law underlies our Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) front prototype.

records.title:
One cooling law.
Two stable phases.
records.text:
Pure atomic H: n = ρ/mH and P/kB = nT. The corrected fit gives isobaric instability between 184.000 and 5039.419 K, corresponding to densities between 0.993567 and 8.681810 cm⁻³. The endpoints are marginal. Dots mark the cold, intermediate and warm intersections at the ZP saturation pressure.PNGSVGEquilibria / CSV
With net volumetric cooling Q = n²Λ − nΓ, thermal equilibrium gives n = Γ/Λ(T) and P/kB = TΓ/Λ(T). Here Γ = 2 × 10⁻²⁶ erg per H atom per second; Λ is in erg cm³ s⁻¹. Let β = d ln Λ / d ln T. At equilibrium, (∂Q/∂T)P = nΓ(β − 1)/T. The local isobaric thermal mode is stable for β > 1 and unstable for β < 1.
These branch labels omit the wavelength dependence of conduction, which stabilizes sufficiently small scales. The isochoric derivative is positive throughout the displayed interval. The plotted 10–10,000 K range is a diagnostic choice, not a claim that a temperature-only fit describes all chemistry or ionization there.
The turning pressures are Pmin/kB = 1597.453 and Pmax/kB = 5007.000 K cm⁻³. Two stable equilibria share a pressure between these limits; a static conductive front imposes an additional condition.

Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), equations (4)–(7), use the same pure-H pressure convention, corrected rates and conductivity. Our two implementations agree on Psat to better than 10⁻¹⁰ relative precision. The paper prints Psat/kB = 2823, Pmax/kB = 5012, and Pmin/kB = 1596 in the text or 1598 in Figure 1. We retain these small numerical differences instead of fitting coefficients to the labels. A nonzero mass flux changes the front problem; uniform thermal equilibrium alone does not determine the pressure–mass-flux classification.

records.section: The coordinate and potential have explicit definitions.
records.text:
Q(T,P) = n²Λ(T) − nΓ, n = (P/kB)/T
κ(T) = 2500 √T
θ(T) = ∫κ(T) dT = (5000/3) T^(3/2)
V(θ(T),P) = ∫[Tcold(P) → T] κ(s) Q(s,P) ds
∂V/∂θ = Q
θ has units erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ and V has units erg² cm⁻⁴ s⁻², the square of an energy flux. V is an effective static-front potential, not the thermodynamic free energy of the gas. Its additive constant is arbitrary; choosing Vcold = 0 makes the difference between the two minima directly visible. The shared scale is Vbarrier,sat = 3.425672655 × 10⁻¹⁸ erg² cm⁻⁴ s⁻².
At a thermal equilibrium, ∂²V/∂θ² = (∂Q/∂T)P / κ. Thus the two isobarically stable equilibria are minima and the unstable intersection is a maximum. A monotonic relabeling from θ to log T preserves these extrema and their depths; it changes the apparent shape and width of the wells.

records.section: Equal depths recover the static-front condition.
records.text:
θ_xx = Q = ∂V/∂θ
(θ_x)² / 2 = V(θ,P) − Vcold
Vwarm − Vcold = ∫[Tcold → Twarm] κ(T) Q(T,P) dT
Zero conductive flux at both endpoints therefore requires equal well depths. This is exactly the existing ZP saturation condition. The independent potential calculation recovers the same pressure and all three thermal-equilibrium intersections. Their temperatures, densities and depths at each pressure are retained in the JSON report.
Verification checks the derivative in θ, the curvature and local extrema of every equilibrium, independent composite Simpson quadrature, refinement from 16,001 to 32,001 quadrature points, the existing ZP integral and the sign of the depth difference. records.text:
Matching a growth-rate curve is only part of the task. The required result is the spatial eigenfunction, with its temperature, velocity, flux and pressure information preserved under one amplitude and phase convention.
This page defines the reconstruction and its acceptance criteria. No Kim2013 background front, eigenvalue, eigenfunction or source digitization has been computed in this project yet. Issue6 tracks the implementation. The original study is Kim & Kim, Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium.

records.title:
Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled.
records.text:
The MU69 example compares temperature and transverse velocity on two different transverse cuts. The reconstruction must produce both curves from the same mode:
Temperature panel: δT/Tbackground at y = 0.5Ly.
Velocity panel: δvy/vx1 at y = 0.25Ly.
Source comparison time: t/tgr = 2; pressure P/kB = 1800 K cm⁻³.
Table3 uses Ly = 1.06 pc; Table1 quotes the fastest wavelength as 1.05 pc. Keep that rounding distinction when selecting k.
Compare signs, extrema, zero crossings, relative amplitudes and far-field decay. Digitization must distinguish the source’s analytical solid curves from its simulation dots, and retain axis calibration and reading uncertainty. A common amplitude alignment can test shape and relative amplitude; matching the absolute amplitude after the source’s initially shifted front requires a separate initial-mode projection or linear initial-value calculation.
The origin is fixed by T = √(T1T2). Temperature divided by Tbackground is a pointwise conversion from the solver’s δT/T1, rather than the same plotted variable.

records.section: Match the paper’s background model first.
records.text:
The source uses the corrected KI cooling fit but a constant conductivity κ = 10⁵ erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ K⁻¹, with m = 1.37mH, n = ρ/m and γ = 5/3. Its reported saturation pressure is Psat/kB = 2282 K cm⁻³. The existing KI/Iwasaki benchmark instead uses κ = 2500√T and has a different computed saturation pressure. Copying its front unchanged would change the problem.
Reconstruct the steady boundary-value problem and its mass-flux eigenvalue from equations (9)–(13), before assembling the linear operator. Figures2–3 and Table1 provide background comparisons. Report residuals against the rounded source values; do not fit coefficients or redefine the origin to force agreement.

records.title:
Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled.
records.text:
xi = x / ell_D1
nu = k ell_D1
sigma = Omega / (k vx1)
state = (J, V, M, Theta, dTheta/dxi)
Theta = temperature Fourier amplitude / T1
AppendixA equations (A7)–(A10) form a five-dimensional first-order problem. The source’s state-vector order differs from the presentation order in (A6); it must be explicit in code. The upstream regular basis contains incompressible and thermal modes. Downstream it contains incompressible, vortex and thermal modes. Match the full state, using the regularity and outgoing-mode conditions of (A11)–(A21).
delta vy / vx1 = Re[ -i V(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ]
delta T / Tbackground
 = (T1/Tbackground) Re[ Theta(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ]
The growing branch may use real state amplitudes; the transverse-velocity Fourier amplitude still carries the explicit −i factor. This gives the transverse phase relation used by the two Figure9 cuts. Independent component normalizations or phase rotations would destroy that information.
Use the paper’s C1 = 1 convention, or a documented equivalent single gauge. Export all five state components, the basis coefficients and reconstructed physical perturbations, with units and the retained approximation order. The source’s low-Mach/isobaric reduction retains hydrodynamic coupling; it must not be replaced by setting pressure and velocity perturbations to zero or advertised as an exact full-compressible spectrum.

records.title:
Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled.
records.text:
Background: converge the thermal front, mass flux and energy balance before solving for perturbations.
Operator: independently check the linearization and heat-loss derivative, and substitute every far-field basis vector into the constant-state equations.
Eigenfunction: retain equation, matching and boundary residuals for all components. Use scale-aware norms without ratios through zero components.
Convergence: enlarge both far fields, refine the spatial representation and tighten tolerances. Both the eigenvalue and the normalized mode shape must converge.
Mode identity: follow the same branch by eigenfunction overlap as k changes. Recover the k = 0 translation mode and long-wave displacement limit without imposing them on finite-k modes.
Source comparison: reconstruct both Figure9 cuts with a common normalization. Validate a representative mode with an independent discretization or small-amplitude linear evolution.
Dispersion: then reproduce Figure5 at P/kB = 1700, 1800 and 1900 K cm⁻³. Its ordinate is ΩellD1/vx1 = νσ, not σ alone. Check (A24), the peak and the cutoff; the downstream vortex tail becomes long as σ approaches zero.
A full nonlinear two-dimensional run is a separate, optional task. The coupled Fourier-mode eigenproblem is the required core.

records.text:
Each work item has a purpose, a completion condition, evidence and a published outcome. An unresolved diagnostic can be useful progress when its assumptions and restart conditions are recorded.
GitHub Issues are the live task record. This page is a dated guide to the current priorities and published work; consult the linked issues for later status changes. We normally keep one scientific implementation active at a time.

records.title:
Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible.
records.text:
The KI2002 static-front potential comparison is implemented, numerically checked and published. It compares 0.9, 1 and 1.1 Psat with a shared normalization: the warm minimum is deeper below saturation, the wells have equal depth at saturation, and the cold minimum is deeper above saturation.
Code, configuration, curve CSV, equilibrium/depth records and desktop/mobile figures accompany the result. Independent quadrature, mesh refinement, derivatives and equilibrium curvatures verify the static correspondence to the ZP condition. No compressible front speed is inferred. Issue1 records the completed scope.

records.title:
Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible.
records.text:
Kim & Kim2013: reconstruct the coupled Figure9 eigenfunctions. The source-audited specification makes component shapes, relative amplitudes, phase and boundary/domain convergence mandatory. This is the next major linear-analysis target now that the KI potential task is complete; no Kim solver has been implemented yet.
Explain pressure-driven compressible flow versus reduced reaction–diffusion models. Retain pressure, momentum, advection and compressional work, while distinguishing nearly uniform pressure from zero flow. Include Chandrasekhar’s Boussinesq convection as an intermediate fluid approximation, with buoyancy as a distinct driver.
Isolate one missing Iwasaki2012 branch or critical-flux example. A bounded trajectory diagnostic comes before another full-grid calculation.
Quantify Schwarz1972 condensation timing and mesh sensitivity. Reuse existing runs and retain source-reading, model and numerical uncertainties.

records.title:

records.text:
Historical simulation gallery: four 2D and four 3D full-frame recordings, an 18-second edited 3D introduction, and two source-traceable still illustrations. Materials MD is excluded. Complete media decode, source/output frame counts and provenance are checked; exact run inputs and paper-figure matches remain unverified. This is archival footage, not a newly validated simulation.
2D thermal-condensation cover: actual compressible evolution, movie, poster, initial/final states and independent numerical benchmarks. Deliberately enhanced conduction broadens interfaces; this is an illustrative model, not a historical reproduction or sustained turbulence.
Field1965 Figures1–3: calculations from the source equations, with numerical checks; pointwise digitized comparisons remain separate work.
KI2002 equilibrium benchmark: corrected coefficients, stability branches, planar ZP saturation and pressure-dependent potential wells with all equilibrium intersections.
Schwarz1972 linear calculation and nonlinear Lagrangian prototype: cooling, conduction and recombination with explicit historical-input and resolution limits.
Iwasaki2012 front-classification prototype: nine source examples agree; the published maps are not fully reproduced.
FGH/GHF equilibrium prototype: original-curve residuals and a conditional saturation search, with historical coefficient recovery deferred.

records.section:
From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation.
records.text:
FGH established a two-phase picture. Later work changed the heating and chemical inputs, then followed fronts, turbulence, and magnetized clouds. This reading list connects those questions to the calculations we can document and explore.
Listed references are not completed reproductions. Bibliography and abstracts have been checked; equations, target figures, and data availability need individual review. This page groups papers by research path; each path runs from oldest to newest. For one chronological list across all paths, open all papers by year. Publication years are used where confirmed, with preprint dates noted separately.

records.title:
From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation.
records.section: Choose the scientific question before the computing budget.
records.text:
Reproducing a large multidimensional simulation can require substantial computing time, storage, and access to original inputs. Our modern-paper exhibits can instead provide a source guide, documented setup, analysis of available outputs, or a small benchmark that isolates a physical mechanism.
Source and method: link the paper and any public code, inputs, and datasets; record what is actually available.
Reuse and analysis: regenerate a diagnostic from released outputs where possible, preserving units, provenance, and processing steps.
Small calculations: evaluate an analytic relation, a one-zone chemical model, a front, or a convergence test within an explicit reduced scope.
Optional full runs: record the resolution, solver, hardware, wall time, and storage needed. A full 2D/3D rerun is not a condition for completing a source or analysis exhibit.
For new nonlinear thermal-instability simulation exhibits, the thermal-conduction treatment and resolution of its relevant scales are selection criteria to audit explicitly. Analytical theory and microphysical rate references are documented separately. Digitized published curves will be identified as digitizations. Reduced models will state their omissions; their results will not be labeled as full-simulation reproductions.

records.section: Foundations: thermal stability, buoyancy and conductive phase exchange
records.text:
Parker (1953) provides a pre-Field historical starting point. Chandrasekhar (1961) supplies the buoyancy-driven convection and Boussinesq comparison. Balbus (1986) extends the local stability analysis to evolving backgrounds, while Begelman & McKee (1990) treats conductive mass exchange between phases. Analytical background references and conduction-resolved simulation exhibits have different roles.

records.section: Global Effects of Thermal Conduction on Two-Phase Media
records.text:
Convection and radiative condensation are distinct: Chandrasekhar’s textbook is included as a foundational monograph, not a journal paper. Its proposed benchmark is buoyancy-driven convection of a layer heated from below. Rayleigh-number onset must not be identified with the cooling-derivative criterion for the Field condensation mode, which does not require gravity.
The Boussinesq comparison retains velocity, a pressure constraint and buoyancy while filtering acoustic compressibility. It does not mean zero flow or zero pressure gradient. The resulting hierarchy for the proposed explanation is: selected reaction–diffusion models → Boussinesq fluid dynamics → compressible thermal gas. These are different approximations and drivers, not a single universal equation.
Spiegel & Veronis (1960), On the Boussinesq Approximation for a Compressible Fluid, gives a primary-source account of its assumptions: a thin layer relative to scale heights and suitably small fluctuations. Density variations remain in the buoyancy force. The compressible-fluid reduction also requires care with the adiabatic temperature gradient.
The textbook’s bibliography is checked; its exact equations, sections and figures are not yet audited because full-text access attempts failed. No textbook figure is claimed reproduced. Source review and proposed scope / JSON.

records.section: Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions
records.text:
Field et al. (1968) discusses Takayanagi and Nishimura’s H₂ excitation data. FGH (1969) cites Hayakawa, Nishimura and Takayanagi’s cosmic-ray heating work. Hattori, Nakano and Hayashi’s reference list includes both papers. These links identify a route for source tracing; they do not establish that later models use identical coefficients.
For each future rate record, we will distinguish cross sections, rate coefficients, energy-loss coefficients, volumetric rates, and yields. Species, colliders, units, normalization, validity range, population assumptions, source equation/table, and correction/code version will accompany the numerical formula.
The Takayanagi–Nishimura rate audit now transcribes 34 coefficients and tests a finite level model. Its Table 2 mismatches remain visible. Other coefficient sets still require equation/table review; the citation links alone do not validate them. Lineage evidence and proposed coefficient-record fields / JSON

records.section: Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions
records.text:
Ionization fraction is a separate branch: Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) calculates electron, ion and charged-grain abundances before magnetic coupling. Figures1–4 compare grain distributions. Figure1 is a possible small charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-balance calculation. Its axes use abundances relative to total hydrogen nuclei and nH/ζ, with ζ the ionization rate per hydrogen molecule; these conventions must not be silently interchanged with FGH’s atomic-gas definitions.
The paper calls Umebayashi & Nakano (1990), Magnetic flux loss from interstellar clouds, MNRAS243,103–113, PaperI and builds on its reaction scheme. The publisher’s abstract confirms an ionization–recombination equilibrium calculation; its full rate-table audit remains pending. Distinguish the ionization rate ζ from the resulting electron fraction, and distinguish both from a cooling coefficient. Source review and parameter conventions / JSON.

Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner (1969) and Penston–Brown (1970) connect to Elphick–Regev–Shaviv (1992), Ferrara–Shchekinov (1993), Shchekinov–Ibáñez (2001), Nagashima and collaborators’ curved-front work, and Kim & Kim’s (2013) conductive evaporation-front instability. Static balance, steady mass flux, perturbations, and spherical survival times are distinct computational questions.

records.section: Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium
records.text:
Gradient-flow connection: Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) gives an isobaric reduction in Lagrangian mass coordinates, a Lyapunov functional, equal-minima ZP fronts and front interactions. The biophysical comparisons follow wave-pinning, conserved protein redistribution and neural excitability, with their distinct conservation laws and scope.
Conductive front instability: Kim & Kim (2013) explicitly includes thermal conduction in the linear stability analysis and nonlinear evolution of evaporation fronts. This provides a comparison with Inoue et al. (2006), while Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) supplies a related steady-front classification. A stability spectrum, a steady-solution classification, and nonlinear saturation are different reproduction targets. The user requires detailed coupled eigenfunctions, especially Figure9, as the Kim2013 reconstruction target; a dispersion curve alone will not complete that task.

records.section: Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium
records.text:
Steady flow and perturbations: Ferrara & Shchekinov (1993) studies static/steady front properties and their dynamical evolution. Shchekinov & Ibáñez (2001) studies planar acoustic/entropy perturbations interacting with steady subsonic fronts. In section 3, Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) explicitly describes the latter work as determining the ZP mass flux j(P) through an eigenvalue problem. We will audit the steady background before attempting perturbation coefficients. This citation does not establish identical cooling laws or numerical parameters.
Related entries: Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama (2006) addresses front stability; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) studies dynamical condensation fronts; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2014) studies interfacial energy transfer in a bistable medium. The Field-condition paper provides a connection to conduction and resolution.
Different heat-loss laws, geometries, and dynamical approximations must be preserved when comparing these studies. A reading path is not proof of identical assumptions or coefficients.

records.text:
The corrected KI2002 equilibrium benchmark includes stability branches, ZP saturation pressure and all three thermal-equilibrium intersections. Model-specific landmarks retain density conventions and unresolved cases. The Maxwell equal-area historical aside traces the primary publications and distinguishes its integral from ZP selection. The same aside develops a scalar Ginzburg–Landau connection, with Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) as a direct precedent.
Field’s stability map connects to front and perturbation problems. FGH/GHF two-phase equilibrium prototype, historical ingredients, and reduced cold branch give a starting point for comparing historical and later microphysics.

records.section:
Let the background cool.

records.text:
Cloud formation can begin while the surrounding gas cools, rather than departing from steady thermal equilibrium. Here the background temperature and ionization evolve together with density perturbations at four wavelengths.
First target: the early-time part of Figure 2. The linear equations include conduction and recombination. Cooling is reconstructed from Figure 1, rather than independently recovered from every atomic rate. The run stops at the input-data boundary, about 1.68 Myr. Late-time Figure 2 remains unfinished. A separate nonlinear Lagrangian prototype now follows the 3 pc, 10% perturbation into condensation.

records.title:

Watch the perturbations grow.
records.section: A time-dependent background changes the instability problem.
records.text:
Solid lines: the declared linear prototype. Dashed black: background temperature, read on the right axis. Open circles: Figure 2 density readings; black crosses: its temperature readings. Gray: beyond the input domain. The right panel shows the reconstructed cooling input. There is no fitted time rescaling.SVGPNGBackground & perturbations / CSVFigure 2 comparison / CSVNumerical report / JSON
Initial conditions: n(H) =0.3 cm⁻³, T =8,200 K, x =n(e)/n(H) =0.05; neutral He/H =0.1. Wavelengths are 0.3,1,3,10 pc. The historical conduction prescription is K(T) =2,500√T in cgs units. No continuing heating is applied.
The 0.3 pc mode initially decreases, showing short-wavelength conduction damping. Within the computed window it later reaches about 14.8 times its initial amplitude, while the 1 pc mode reaches about 107. The latter maximum occurs at the domain stop and is not an established peak. These are normalized linear amplitudes, not nonlinear cloud density contrasts.
The original curves are not matched exactly. The report gives separate log-RMS discrepancies and scored-point counts for temperature and each wavelength. Points past the domain stop have no model prediction. These descriptive differences are not numerical pass tolerances.

records.section: Integrate the background and perturbations together.
records.text:
Equations (16)–(18) evolve uniform cooling and recombination. Equations (19)–(24) evolve relative density, pressure, velocity divergence, and ionization perturbations; the equation of state supplies the temperature perturbation. The coefficients change with time, so a single constant exponential growth rate is insufficient.
d ln T₀/dt = −1/τC + (2−γ)[x₀/(1.1+x₀)]/τR
d ln x₀/dt = −1/τR
τC = (1.1+x₀)kT₀ / [n₀(γ−1)Λ]
τR = 1/[n₀x₀α⁽²⁾(T₀)]
The pressure perturbation contains the conduction term in equation (19). Density amplitudes are normalized to n₁(0) =1; the actual perturbation may be arbitrarily small. Pressure, velocity and relative ionization perturbations initially vanish. This declared initial-mode choice has not been confirmed as the unique Figure 2 initialization.
DOP 853 and Radau agree on the computed evolution. Equation (19) is also compared with a centered-difference Jacobian of the original primitive pressure equation, including the changing background normalization.

records.section: Keep the historical input limits visible.
records.text:
The 39 Figure 1 readings cover x =0.001,0.01,0.1 and T ≈13.93–8,429.74 K. PCHIP interpolates logΛ(logT), with Λ piecewise linear in ionization fraction. A logarithmic-ionization alternative changes the stopping time to about 1.51 Myr, illustrating reconstruction sensitivity.
The accepted solution stops at the lowest supported temperature,13.93 K, after 1.679 Myr. It is not continued through an invented cold cooling law. Raw pixels, crop origins, calibration ticks and source hashes accompany the input. Figure 2 readings use the 0–2 Myr ticks bracketing the sampled interval; a single exact affine scale is not assumed for the slightly distorted full scan. Reading envelopes are practical limits, not statistical confidence intervals, and there is no independent second digitization.
H recombination uses Hjellming’s (1966) excited-state approximation; the exact fit used by Schwarz and collaborators remains unidentified. Nonpositive linear amplitudes remain in the CSV but are omitted from the log plot; they do not mean negative physical gas density.
This paper adopts Fe/H =5 ×10⁻⁵, compared with 8 ×10⁻⁶ in the earlier FGH baseline. Neither FGH nor KI cooling is silently substituted. Jura & Dalgarno’s Table 1 supplies several electron-impact rates but does not alone specify all required neutral channels.

records.text:
A 10% density wave grows beyond the linear regime in a cooling 3 pc box. Moving mass cells follow the compression, while thermal conduction, recombination and shock heating act together.
A nonlinear numerical prototype, using 96 mass cells for the displayed profiles. There is no Riemann solver. The method uses pressure forces, compatible pressure work and compression-only artificial viscosity. Figures 3–6 motivate the outputs; original cooling inputs, timing and front resolution remain imperfect, so this is not certified historical reproduction.

records.title:
Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer.
records.text:
Times are the same as the published snapshots; no temporal or phase shift was fitted. The displayed run uses 96 equal-H-mass cells. Both the mass coordinate and physical positions/cell widths are exported. The original figure labels zone number; its exact grid-to-mass mapping has not been recovered.Profiles / SVGPNGFull profiles / CSVMesh histories / CSVValidation & source comparison / JSON
At 0.985 Myr the displayed model has peak n(H) ≈ 31.1 cm⁻³, a density contrast ≈ 187, minimum temperature ≈ 12.7 K and minimum ionization fraction ≈ 0.0010. The surrounding warm minimum-density gas is about 1430 K. These are computed quantities, not prescribed cloud conditions.
The paper’s text gives approximate cloud values of 15 K, x ≈ 0.002, a 0.007 pc extent and 20% of the mass, with an intercloud temperature about 1,800 K. Our density-excess FWHM is 0.0078 pc, while the broader selection T < 100 K and n > 10 times the mean gives 0.0155 pc and 28.1% of the mass. These definitions need not coincide with the original cloud edge.
The condensation timing differs: by 0.955 Myr this prototype already has a strongly condensed layer, whereas the corresponding original profile is still growing. The resemblance of the late cloud does not establish pointwise agreement throughout the evolution.

records.title:
Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer.
records.text:
The periodic domain contains a sinusoidal physical-space density perturbation of amplitude 0.1 and wavelength 3 pc, with mean n(H) = 0.3 cm⁻³. The unperturbed temperature is 8,200 K, x = 0.05, and neutral He/H = 0.1. Initial pressure is uniform, so the local temperature varies inversely with density; velocities start at zero.
Equal-H-mass cells move with the gas. A compatible midpoint pressure-work update balances changes in internal and kinetic energy. Compression-only quadratic and linear artificial viscosity handle shocks. Conduction uses a conservative periodic implicit solve, and a coupled local energy/recombination solve accounts for radiative losses and changing particle number.
This is not the recovered original program. The paper describes von Neumann–Richtmyer viscosity and 100–200 spatial mesh points. The 64/96-cell cases explore historical-scale calculations below that reported range; the 128-cell case lies within it. We keep these experiments separate from any claim about the authors’ exact mesh.
The semi-implicit conduction update is backward Euler. We therefore do not claim global second-order time accuracy; timestep refinement is measured directly. No temperature floor, clipped density, imposed cold layer or fitted time shift is used.

records.section: Compare mesh counts without declaring every front resolved.
records.text:
64, 96 and 128 cells are the historical-scale study; 512 cells provide an auxiliary comparison. The dashed temperature line is the input boundary. The four-cell Field-length line is a stated diagnostic, not a universal theorem, and is not met throughout these runs.Mesh comparison / SVGPNG
At 0.985 Myr the 96-to-128 density-profile L1 difference on mass coordinate is about 3.2%; 128 versus 512 differs by about 4.7%. Halving the timestep in the 96-cell calculation changes the density profile by about 0.02%. Profiles are compared without shifting the cloud.
Spatial front resolution is still limited. The auxiliary 512-cell run reaches a minimum Field-length proxy of only 1.37 cells. The proxy is √[K(T)T/(n²Λ)]. A small difference between these cloud profiles is not proof that the thin conductive interface or a continuum solution is fully resolved.
All 33 numerical self-checks pass, including compatible hydro energy accounting, a periodic conduction Fourier mode, independent cooling/recombination ODEs, the small-amplitude linear limit, box length, momentum, positivity and timestep agreement. The unmet spatial-resolution diagnostic is recorded separately and is not counted as a passed check.

records.section: Track where the cooling input is extended.
records.text:
The nonlinear cooling table adds 12 warm-end readings to the earlier 39 points from Figure 1. These cover the locally warmer cells in the initially isobaric wave. The earlier linear input and results are preserved.
Below the lowest graph temperature, about 13.93 K, the model uses a continuous C II-like asymptote with exp(−92/T), neutral-collider T⁰ and electron-collider T⁻¹ᐟ² factors. Below x = 0.001 the two low-ionization curves continue to a nonnegative neutral-collider contribution. These are explicit extrapolations, not recovered historical coefficients.
The 96-cell density contrast first reaches 100 near 0.948 Myr. It enters the cold temperature extension near 0.974 Myr and the low-ionization extension near 0.986 Myr. Thus the initial formation of the high-contrast layer precedes those extensions, while the later cloud state depends on them. Exposure of each accepted state is recorded in the report.
Changing the cold electron temperature power from −1/2 to 0 is included as a sensitivity probe. It does not bound every uncertainty in the historical cooling rates. The recombination fit, normalization caveat and proof note described in the linear exhibit remain relevant.

records.title:

records.section:
Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling.
records.text:
Before a cooling function becomes one line of code, it depends on collision partners, transition directions, level populations, and radiative losses. Here we trace those steps through a historical H₂ calculation.
Scope: 34 printed excitation coefficients and a declared finite-level calculation, compared with 60 printed cooling values. This is not a complete reproduction of the original cooling model. Numerical checks and differences from the source table are reported separately.

records.title:
Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling.
records.section: From H-atom collisions to para-H₂ radiation.
records.text:
Table 1, printed p. 82: thermally averaged upward excitation coefficients. The right panel uses those coefficients, equations (7) and (9), and the photon-energy definition on p. 83. Lines connect computed samples, while crosses show the source cooling values. No interpolated coefficients enter the calculation.SVGPNG34 rate records / CSVLevel populations & cooling / CSV
The coefficient qup has units cm³ s⁻¹. It counts excitations per collider–target pair; it is not yet an energy-loss coefficient. To obtain radiation, we must also determine the excited-state population and the energy carried by a decay.
These are the temperatures and channels printed in the 1960 source. The authors discuss limitations of their collision approximation and temperature-dependent accuracy; numerical reproduction of a coefficient does not establish that it is an accurate modern rate.

records.title:
Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling.
records.section: Keep upward rates, downward rates, and energy losses distinct.
records.text:
qdown = qup [(2J−3)/(2J+1)] exp[170.68(2J−1)/T]
pJ/pJ−2 = n(H)qup / [n(H)qdown + AJ→J−2]
L / n(para-H₂) = ΣJ pJAJ→J−2ΔEJ,J−2
J denotes the upper state of a pair of adjacent even rotational levels. The population fractions sum to one. n(H) is the H-atom collider density, rather than the total hydrogen-nuclei density. The final cooling is in erg s⁻¹ per para-H₂ molecule; multiplying by its number density gives erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹.
The historical spontaneous-emission formula is A = 7.52 × 10⁻¹³ J(J−1)(2J−1)⁴/(2J+1) s⁻¹. The photon energy is ΔE = 2.3561 × 10⁻¹⁴(2J−1) erg. Both are retained as printed, without substituting modern coefficients.

records.title:
Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling.
records.section: What does a blank table entry mean?
records.text:
Table 1 provides fewer transitions at lower temperatures. Its missing entries are preserved as unavailable inputs. At each temperature this experiment closes the ladder at the highest connected level for which an upward coefficient is listed: J = 2, 4, 6, or 8.
That is an explicit truncation of the model. It does not establish a zero physical rate to higher levels. The calculation includes H-atom collisions, para-H₂, and optically thin spontaneous emission at fixed gas temperature. It does not include ortho-H₂, other colliders, line trapping, gas chemistry, or a gas thermal-equilibrium solution.

records.section: Show the mismatch as part of the result.
records.text:
100 × (finite-ladder calculation / printed cooling − 1), for 60 reference points. These are measured discrepancies, not passed validation tests. The source row that appears as 155 K in Table 2, while Table 1 gives 150 K, is excluded pending clarification.SVGPNGPrinted values & differences / CSV
The largest discrepancy is at T = 200 K and n(H) = 100 cm⁻³. The restricted calculation gives 4.6578 × 10⁻²⁵ erg s⁻¹ per molecule, compared with 5.95 × 10⁻²⁵ in the printed table: a difference of approximately −21.72%.
We have not established the cause. Additional level/rate information or a source correction may be needed before assigning an explanation. The input coefficients are left unchanged, and the discrepancy remains in the downloadable comparison.
